name: Theravada Buddhism
era: From the 3rd century BCE to today
line: Keep the precepts, steady the mind and see for yourself how things are.

quote.text: Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought.

quotes.text: Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.
To avoid all evil, to cultivate good, and to cleanse one’s mind: this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
Even as a mother protects with her life her child, her only child, so with a boundless heart should one cherish all living beings.
quotes.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8, trans. the Amaravati Sangha

quotes.text: All conditioned things are subject to decay. Strive on with diligence.
quotes.source: His last words, Maha-parinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16, in a common English rendering

quotes.text: Do everything with a mind that lets go.
quotes.source: A Still Forest Pool, ed. Jack Kornfield and Paul Breiter, 1985

words.usage: The oldest surviving school of Buddhism, which keeps its scriptures in the Pali language.

words.meaning: The teaching; the truth; the way things are
words.usage: The Pali form of the Sanskrit dharma. The second of the three refuges.
A title. Theravada honours Gotama as a human being who found the path and taught it.
Strictly the order of monks and nuns, and all who have reached the stages of awakening.
The first training and the ground for the other two. For lay people, the five precepts.
A mind gathered and steady on one object. The second training.
Seeing impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self directly. The third training.
The first noble truth. Nothing that changes can be finally relied on.
Everything that arises passes away. The first of the three marks of existence.
Nothing in body or mind can be found that is a lasting owner or essence.
Literally thirst. The second noble truth names it as the origin of suffering.
The going out of the fires of greed, hatred and delusion. Nirvana in Sanskrit.
The Buddha defined it as intention. What one chooses shapes what one becomes.
Friendliness toward all beings without exception. The first of the four sublime states.
The trembling of the heart at another’s pain.
Gladness at someone else’s success. The cure for envy.
Balance of mind in gain and loss, praise and blame.
Remembering to be present with what is happening. The word also means memory.
The meditation the Buddha is said to have used on the night of his awakening.
Clear seeing into the three marks. Also the name of the modern lay meditation movement.
The Pali word usually translated as meditation. It means making something grow.
The first practice taught to lay people, and the one that feeds the monks every day.
The good that results from giving, virtue and meditation. Tham bun, making merit, is the centre of Thai lay religion.
One who lives on alms, under 227 rules. A nun is a bhikkhuni.
The monastic code, the first of the three baskets of scripture.
A teaching of the Buddha or a close disciple. The second basket holds several thousand.
The days of the full, new and quarter moons, when lay people keep eight precepts and visit the monastery.
The centre of village life in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia: school, meeting hall and place of merit.
Said three times at the end of a chant or a teaching, in approval and thanks.
Care and diligence. The quality the Buddha urged in his last words.

practices.name: The five precepts at dawn
practices.instructions: Sit upright with your palms together. Recollect the three things Buddhists rely on: an awakened teacher, his teaching and the community that keeps it. Then undertake the five precepts for today, one at a time, in your own words: I will not kill. I will not take what is not given. I will not misuse sex. I will not lie. I will not cloud my mind with drink or drugs. They are undertakings you choose, and you make them afresh each day.
practices.why: Lay Buddhists across Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia recite these five most mornings and at every ceremony. Virtue comes first because a mind without remorse settles easily.
variations: On one day a week add the eighth-precept habit of not eating after midday.
Chant them in Pali from a recording.
At night check each of the five against the day.

practices.name: Mindfulness of breathing
practices.instructions: Sit on a cushion or a chair with your back straight and your hands in your lap. Close your eyes. Find the place where the breath is clearest, at the nostrils or the belly, and rest your attention there. Know a long breath as long and a short breath as short. Do not control it. When you find you have been thinking, note that, let it go and return to the next breath. Begin with fifteen minutes and add a little each week.
practices.why: This is anapanasati, set out by the Buddha in sixteen steps in the Middle Length Discourses. It calms the mind and is the usual base for insight.
variations: Count breaths from one to ten and start again.
Sit for five minutes at midday as well.
Try it lying down before sleep, staying awake.

practices.name: Dana: give food
practices.instructions: Each day give food to someone before you eat your own main meal. Cook an extra portion for a neighbour, buy lunch for a colleague, leave food at a food bank, feed birds. Give with your own hand where you can, respectfully and without making anything of it. Afterwards notice the state of your mind.
practices.why: At dawn across the Theravada world people stand at the roadside to put rice in the bowls of passing monks. The Buddha taught giving first because generosity loosens the grip of craving.
variations: Give money you had planned to spend on yourself.
Give time to someone who needs help.
If there is a monastery near you, ask how to offer a meal.

practices.name: Walking meditation
practices.instructions: Find a straight path of about twenty paces, indoors or out. Stand at one end and feel your feet. Walk to the other end slowly, eyes lowered, hands held together in front, attention on the lifting, moving and placing of each foot. Stop, stand, turn and walk back. When the mind wanders, stop walking until it returns.
practices.why: Forest monks spend hours each day on such a path. The Buddha walked up and down in the open at dawn. It trains mindfulness in movement and suits a restless mind.
variations: Walk at normal speed to the shops with the same attention.
Walk for ten minutes directly after eating.

practices.name: Loving-kindness at night
practices.instructions: Sit or lie comfortably. Begin with yourself: may I be safe, may I be well, may I be at ease. Then bring to mind in turn someone who has helped you, a friend, a person you hardly know, a person you find difficult, and finally all beings in every direction, and wish each of them the same. Go slowly. Where the wish will not come, stay with that person a little longer and do not force it.
practices.why: The Metta Sutta asks for a heart as wide as a mother’s for her only child, extended to every being. It is chanted nightly in monasteries and is the standard remedy for ill will.
variations: Send it only to the difficult person for a week.
Do it on the bus for each passenger.
End by sharing the good of the day with those who have died.

tasks.name: Eat your last meal before midday, once this week
tasks.meta: The uposatha habit; skip if unwise for your health

tasks.name: Read the first two chapters of the Dhammapada
Listen to the Metta Sutta chanted in Pali
Look at the reclining Buddha of Gal Vihara
Sit in silence for ten minutes after sunset with no device in the room
Cook rice and a simple curry and share it
tasks.meta: Eat · give the first portion away

tasks.name: Journal: what did you crave today, and what happened to it?
The three marks: watch one pleasant thing end
Carry an insect outside instead of killing it

rules.why: Kill nothing on purpose today, down to the mosquito. Put the spider outside.

rules.text: Take nothing that is not given
rules.why: No borrowed pens kept, no time stolen from an employer, no credit for someone else’s work.

rules.text: Speak only what is true and useful
rules.why: No lies, no gossip, no harsh words, no idle chatter. Silence is always allowed.
No alcohol and no intoxicants for the length of the Onda. The fifth precept protects the other four.
Offer food, money or help to someone every day before your own main meal.
Twenty minutes with the breath, at the same time and place, whether it goes well or badly.

read.title: The Dhammapada
read.creator: trans. Acharya Buddharakkhita, or Gil Fronsdal
read.why: Four hundred and twenty-three verses, the best loved book in the Pali canon. Read a chapter a day.

read.title: In the Buddha’s Words
read.creator: ed. and trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi
read.why: An anthology of the discourses arranged by theme, with clear introductions. The best single way into the canon.

read.title: What the Buddha Taught
read.creator: Walpola Rahula
read.why: A Sri Lankan scholar-monk sets out the four truths, not-self and meditation in a hundred plain pages.

read.title: A Still Forest Pool
read.creator: Ajahn Chah, ed. Jack Kornfield and Paul Breiter
read.why: Short talks by the Thai forest master: earthy, funny and direct.

read.title: The Heart of Buddhist Meditation
read.creator: Nyanaponika Thera
read.why: The book that introduced the practice of mindfulness to the West, by a German monk who lived in Sri Lanka.

read.title: Mindfulness in Plain English
read.creator: Bhante Henepola Gunaratana
read.why: A practical manual for sitting, written by a Sri Lankan monk. Free to read online.

watch.title: Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives
watch.creator: Apichatpong Weerasethakul
watch.why: A dying man in north-east Thailand is visited by ghosts and memories of other lives. Rebirth as ordinary country fact.

watch.title: The Burmese Harp
watch.creator: Kon Ichikawa
watch.why: A Japanese soldier in Burma at the end of the war puts on a monk’s robe and stays to bury the dead.

watch.title: Doing Time, Doing Vipassana
watch.creator: Ayelet Menahemi and Eilona Ariel
watch.why: A documentary on ten-day silent meditation courses held for inmates in Tihar Jail in Delhi.

watch.title: The Buddha
watch.creator: David Grubin, PBS
watch.why: A two-hour documentary life of the Buddha with poets, monks and scholars.

listen.title: Pali chanting: the Metta, Mangala and Ratana Suttas
listen.creator: Sri Lankan pirith; many recordings
listen.why: The three protective discourses chanted through the night at blessings, with a thread passed from hand to hand.

listen.title: Morning and evening chanting
listen.creator: Amaravati or Abhayagiri Buddhist Monastery
listen.why: The daily office of the Thai forest tradition, in Pali and English. Free on the monastery websites.

listen.title: Dhamma talks
listen.creator: Ajahn Brahm, Ajahn Sumedho, Bhikkhu Bodhi and others
listen.why: Thousands of hours of teaching given freely, as the teaching has always been.

listen.title: Piphat ensemble music
listen.creator: Thai classical musicians
listen.why: Gongs, xylophones and oboe: the ceremonial music of Thai and Cambodian temples.

art.title: Gal Vihara
art.creator: Polonnaruwa, Sri Lanka
art.why: Four figures of the Buddha cut from a single granite wall: seated, standing and a fourteen-metre reclining figure at the moment of final release.

art.title: Walking Buddha
art.creator: Sukhothai, Thailand
art.why: The Sukhothai sculptors invented a Buddha in mid-stride, boneless and flame-topped, unlike anything in India.

art.title: The temples of Bagan
art.creator: Myanmar
art.why: More than two thousand brick temples and stupas across a plain by the Irrawaddy. Many hold murals of the Buddha’s past lives.

art.title: The Great Stupa at Sanchi
art.creator: Madhya Pradesh, India
art.why: An early relic mound with four carved gateways. The Buddha is shown only by signs: a tree, a wheel, footprints, an empty seat.

eat.title: Rice and curry
eat.creator: Rice with dal, a vegetable curry and coconut sambol
eat.why: The Sri Lankan everyday plate and the standard offering to monks.

eat.title: Sticky rice
eat.creator: Steamed glutinous rice eaten by hand
eat.why: What is placed in the monks’ bowls each dawn in Laos and north-east Thailand.

eat.title: Kiribath
eat.creator: Rice cooked in coconut milk and cut in diamonds
eat.why: Milk rice, made in Sri Lanka for new year and every auspicious beginning. It recalls the milk rice Sujata gave the Buddha before his awakening.

eat.title: Mohinga
eat.creator: Rice noodles in fish broth with lemongrass and banana stem
eat.why: The breakfast of Myanmar. Lay Theravada Buddhists are not required to be vegetarian, and monks eat what is given.

drink.title: Plain tea
drink.creator: Black tea, unsweetened
drink.why: Sri Lanka grows some of the best. A flask of tea is the usual welcome in a monastery.

drink.title: Water, drunk with attention
drink.creator: A full glass
drink.why: After midday, those keeping eight precepts take only liquids. Water tastes different when it is the meal.

drink.title: Fresh coconut water
drink.creator: From a green coconut
drink.why: Offered to monks in the afternoon and to visitors everywhere from Sri Lanka to Cambodia.

customs.title: The alms round
customs.creator: Dawn
customs.why: Monks walk barefoot and silent with their bowls. Lay people kneel or stand, shoes off, and place food in each bowl. The monks do not thank them, since the giver is the one who gains.

customs.title: Three bows
customs.creator: To the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha
customs.why: Kneeling, with palms together at the forehead and then flat on the floor. Visitors may simply sit quietly.

customs.title: Feet and heads
customs.creator: Sitting in a shrine hall
customs.why: Do not point your feet at a Buddha image or a monk. Sit lower than a monk. Women do not hand things directly to monks in Thailand.

customs.title: Temporary ordination
customs.creator: A few weeks or months in robes
customs.why: In Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia most men become monks for a short time, often in their twenties, to make merit for their parents.

games.title: Makruk
games.creator: Board game · Thailand
games.why: Thai chess, close to the ancient Indian game. Slower and more patient than the Western form. Cambodia plays a near twin called ouk.

games.title: Chinlone
games.creator: Ball game · Myanmar
games.why: A circle of players keeps a woven cane ball in the air with feet and knees. There are no teams and no score. The aim is grace.

games.title: Mandala
games.creator: Board game · Trevor Benjamin and Brett J. Gilbert
games.why: A quiet two-player card game on a cloth mat, named after the sand pictures that are made and swept away. A light lesson in impermanence.

festivals.title: Vesak
festivals.creator: Full moon of May
festivals.why: The Buddha’s birth, awakening and death, all on one day. Lanterns, alms and free food stalls in Sri Lanka.

festivals.title: The Rains Retreat (Vassa)
festivals.creator: July to October, three lunar months
festivals.why: Monks stay in one monastery to study and meditate. Many lay people give up something for the season. It ends with the offering of robes, Kathina.

festivals.title: Songkran and Thingyan
festivals.creator: Mid-April
festivals.why: The new year in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar. Buddha images are bathed, elders have water poured on their hands, and everyone gets soaked.

festivals.title: Poson
festivals.creator: Full moon of June
festivals.why: Sri Lanka marks the arrival of Buddhism with the monk Mahinda. Pilgrims in white climb the rock at Mihintale.

places.title: Anuradhapura
places.creator: North Central Province, Sri Lanka
places.why: The ancient capital, with vast brick stupas and the Sri Maha Bodhi, a tree grown from a cutting of the one the Buddha sat under. Wear white and cover knees and shoulders.

places.title: Shwedagon Pagoda
places.creator: Yangon, Myanmar
places.why: A gilded stupa a hundred metres high, ringed by shrines. Go at dusk. Check current travel advice for Myanmar before planning.

places.title: Luang Prabang
places.creator: Laos
places.why: A small royal town where hundreds of monks walk for alms at dawn. Watch from a distance or take part properly. Do not use flash.

places.title: Wat Pah Nanachat
places.creator: Ubon Ratchathani, Thailand
places.why: The international forest monastery founded by Ajahn Chah for English-speaking monks. Guests may stay by arrangement and follow the routine.

places.title: Bodh Gaya
places.creator: Bihar, India
places.why: The place of the awakening. Temples of every Buddhist country surround the Mahabodhi Temple and the tree.

ethics.title: The five precepts
ethics.text: No killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying or intoxication. They are called training rules, taken on freely. Kept well, they are said to give others the gift of safety.
ethics.practice: Choose the precept you find hardest and keep it perfectly for one day.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: Giving is the first of the ten perfections. It is practised daily, in small amounts, until the hand opens by itself.
ethics.practice: Give something today the moment the thought of giving arises, before the second thought.

ethics.title: Right speech
ethics.text: Speech should be true, kind, useful and timely. The Buddha said he would say what was unwelcome only if it was also true and beneficial, and then he chose his moment.
ethics.practice: Before speaking in one conversation today, ask: is it true, is it kind, is it the time.

ethics.title: Right livelihood
ethics.text: Earn a living without trading in weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants or poison, and without deceit.
ethics.practice: Look honestly at how your income is made. Name one thing you could do more cleanly.

ethics.title: Gratitude to parents and teachers
ethics.text: The Buddha said that a child could carry both parents on their shoulders for a hundred years and still not repay them.
ethics.practice: Do something today for a parent, or for whoever raised you, or in their memory.

ethics.title: Harmlessness
ethics.text: Ill will harms the one who holds it first. Meeting hatred with non-hatred is called an ancient law.
ethics.practice: Let one provocation pass today without a reply.

philosophy.title: The four noble truths
philosophy.text: There is suffering. It has a cause, which is craving. It can end. There is a path to its ending. The Buddha presented himself as a doctor: diagnosis, cause, prognosis and cure.
philosophy.practice: Take one thing that troubled you today and find the wanting underneath it.

philosophy.title: The noble eightfold path
philosophy.text: Right view and intention; right speech, action and livelihood; right effort, mindfulness and concentration. Wisdom, virtue and meditation are trained together, each supporting the others.
philosophy.practice: Pick the limb of the path you have most neglected. Do one thing for it today.

philosophy.title: Impermanence
philosophy.text: Everything that begins ends: a sound, a mood, a body, a civilisation. Seen clearly, this loosens grasping. The fact is plain enough, and the practice is to see it as it happens.
philosophy.practice: Watch one pleasant experience from start to finish and notice the moment it goes.

philosophy.title: Not-self
philosophy.text: Search the body, feelings, perceptions, intentions and awareness and you will not find an owner who stays the same. The self is a process, like a river or a flame.
philosophy.practice: When a strong emotion comes today, say there is anger in place of I am angry.

philosophy.title: Kamma is intention
philosophy.text: It is the choice behind an act that counts, and choices repeated become character. You are, the texts say, the owner and heir of your actions.
philosophy.practice: Before one action today, stop and ask what you are really intending.

philosophy.title: Come and see
philosophy.text: The teaching is described as inviting inspection. The Buddha told the Kalamas to rely on what they found by experience to lead to harm or to welfare.
philosophy.practice: Take one claim from this Onda and test it for a week before deciding.

philosophy.title: The middle way
philosophy.text: The Buddha had tried luxury and self-starvation and rejected both. The path runs between indulgence and harshness, like a lute string tuned neither too tight nor too slack.
philosophy.practice: Find where you are too tight today and where too slack. Adjust one.

philosophy.title: Heedfulness
philosophy.text: The last words of the Buddha were an instruction to be diligent. Mindfulness is called the path to the deathless, and carelessness the path of death.
philosophy.practice: Do one routine task today, such as washing up, with complete care.

intro: Theravada means the teaching of the elders. It is the oldest school of Buddhism still in existence and the religion of most people in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, some 150 million in all. It keeps the earliest complete collection of the Buddha’s teaching, the Pali canon, and holds closely to what it finds there.

The Buddha it honours is a human being: Siddhattha Gotama, born on the edge of the Himalayas about twenty-five centuries ago, who left a comfortable home, tried and abandoned extreme self-denial, and at thirty-five sat under a tree and saw how suffering arises and how it ends. He spent forty-five years walking the Ganges plain teaching what he had found and founding an order of monks and nuns to carry it on.

What he taught fits in a sentence: suffering comes from craving, and craving can be brought to an end by a path of virtue, meditation and wisdom. Theravada lays that path out carefully. First come the precepts and generosity, which make a life blameless. Then comes the training of attention, by mindfulness of breathing and other methods. On that base grows insight into three facts about all experience: it is impermanent, it cannot finally satisfy, and no part of it is a lasting self.

The tradition rests on a partnership. Monks and nuns own almost nothing, eat one or two meals before noon from what they are given, and devote themselves to study and practice. Lay people feed and clothe them, keep five precepts, visit the monastery on moon days and make merit by giving. Each side depends on the other every morning, at the alms round. Many men and some women ordain for a short time.

In the twentieth century, teachers in Burma and Thailand opened serious meditation to lay people. The worldwide interest in mindfulness and in silent retreats comes largely from them, and from forest masters such as Ajahn Chah whose Western students founded monasteries abroad.

This Onda follows the lay Buddhist’s day. You will undertake the five precepts each morning, sit with the breath, give food before you eat, walk with attention and end the day with loving-kindness. You are a guest of the tradition. Taking refuge formally, and deeper meditation, are best done with a teacher. If strong distress comes up while sitting, stop and seek advice.
guide.origin: North India, then Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia
guide.era: The school took shape in Sri Lanka from the 3rd century BCE and has an unbroken monastic line

figures.name: Siddhattha Gotama, the Buddha
figures.dates: about 480 to 400 BCE; traditional dates are earlier
figures.bio: The teacher. Theravada stresses that he was a man who woke up by his own effort and showed that others can.

figures.name: Ananda
figures.bio: The Buddha’s cousin and attendant for twenty-five years, who remembered the discourses and persuaded him to ordain women.

figures.name: Mahapajapati Gotami
figures.bio: The Buddha’s aunt and foster mother. She walked barefoot with five hundred women to ask for ordination and became the first nun.

figures.name: Ashoka
figures.bio: The Indian emperor who turned to the Dhamma after a bloody conquest, carved edicts on rock urging tolerance and sent missions abroad.

figures.name: Mahinda and Sanghamitta
figures.bio: Ashoka’s son and daughter, by tradition. He brought the teaching to Sri Lanka and she brought the order of nuns and a cutting of the Bodhi tree.

figures.name: Buddhaghosa
figures.bio: An Indian monk in Sri Lanka whose Path of Purification is the great handbook of Theravada doctrine and meditation.

figures.name: Mahasi Sayadaw
figures.bio: A Burmese scholar-monk whose method of noting each experience made intensive insight meditation available to lay people worldwide.

figures.name: Ajahn Chah
figures.bio: A Thai forest monk of great simplicity and humour. His monastery Wat Nong Pah Pong has more than three hundred branches.

figures.name: Dipa Ma
figures.bio: A Bengali widow and mother who learned meditation in Burma and taught from a small flat in Calcutta. Many Western teachers were her students.

history.detail: He awakens at Bodh Gaya, gives his first discourse in the deer park at Sarnath and dies at Kusinara aged eighty.
Five hundred senior monks meet at Rajagaha to recite the discourses and the discipline. The teaching is fixed in memory and passed on by group chanting.
The emperor supports the order. A council at Pataliputra is said to settle doctrine, and missions go out in nine directions.
King Devanampiya Tissa meets the monk Mahinda on the hill of Mihintale. The Great Monastery is founded at Anuradhapura and becomes the home of the Theravada.
During famine and war, monks at the Aluvihara rock temple write the Pali scriptures on palm leaves for the first time.
He translates the old Sinhala commentaries into Pali and writes the Path of Purification. Theravada orthodoxy takes the form it still has.
King Anawrahta of Burma adopts Theravada. Over two centuries his dynasty builds thousands of temples on the plain of Bagan.
The Thai kingdom of Sukhothai and then Lan Xang and the Khmer adopt the Sri Lankan lineage. It has been the religion of the region since.
King Mindon of Burma has the whole canon inscribed on 729 marble slabs at Mandalay, often called the world’s largest book.
Founded in London by T. W. Rhys Davids to edit and translate the canon. Buddhists in Asia and scholars in Europe begin to work together.

history.what: Lay meditation and the forest revival
history.detail: Ledi Sayadaw in Burma teaches insight to lay people. In Thailand Ajahn Mun revives the wandering forest life.
Monks from all Theravada countries meet in Rangoon to recite and print an agreed text of the canon, 2,500 years after the Buddha by traditional count.
The full ordination of women, which had died out in Theravada about a thousand years ago, is revived in Sri Lanka. It remains disputed in Thailand and Myanmar.

concepts.detail: A person becomes a Buddhist by going for refuge to these three. They are the teacher, the teaching and the community of those who have realised it.

concepts.text: The frame of the whole teaching.
concepts.detail: Suffering, its origin, its cessation and the path. Each comes with a task: to understand, to abandon, to realise and to develop.
The characteristics of everything conditioned. Insight meditation consists of seeing them in one’s own body and mind, moment by moment.
A chain of twelve links, from ignorance through craving and clinging to birth and death. When one link is cut, the chain stops.

concepts.text: What a person is made of.
concepts.detail: Body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. Each is examined and found to be changing and ownerless.
The eightfold path grouped into three stages. Each depends on the one before, as a house needs foundations before a roof.

concepts.text: One who has finished the work.
concepts.detail: A person in whom greed, hatred and delusion are extinguished. The goal of the Theravada path, reached in four stages beginning with stream-entry.
Also called the divine abidings. Each is developed in meditation and extended without limit.

concepts.text: The good that good deeds bring.
concepts.detail: Made by giving, virtue and meditation, and shared with the dead and with all beings by pouring water or by a spoken wish.

facts.text: The Pali canon in its printed Thai edition fills forty-five volumes, and some Burmese monks have memorised all of it. The first to do so in modern times was Mingun Sayadaw in 1954.
The Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura, planted in the third century BCE, is the oldest living tree with a known planting date.
Monks do not eat after midday, do not handle money and may own only eight things by rule, among them three robes, a bowl, a razor and a needle.
The colour of robes depends on the dye and the lineage: saffron in Thailand, maroon in Myanmar, ochre brown among forest monks.
The Buddhist flag of six coloured stripes was designed in Colombo in 1885 and is now flown worldwide.
In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia the calendar counts years from the Buddha’s death, so 2026 is 2569.

glossary.meaning: The Middle Indian language of the Theravada scriptures
The three baskets: discipline, discourses and higher teaching
A domed monument holding relics; a pagoda, chedi or dagoba
Teacher: the Thai title for a senior monk
Royal teacher: the Burmese title for a senior monk
One of the 547 stories of the Buddha’s earlier lives

furtherReading.title: Theravada Buddhism: A Social History from Ancient Benares to Modern Colombo

sensitivity.note: Theravada Buddhism is a living religion with an unbroken monastic community. This Onda offers the ordinary practices of lay Buddhists. It does not replace a teacher, and intensive meditation is best begun with guidance.
requiredCaveats: Customs vary between Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, and between village and forest monasteries.
Buddha images are sacred. In several countries using them as decoration or tattoos is offensive and may be illegal.
Not eating after midday is optional here and unsuitable for some people. Put your health first.
Meditation can bring up difficult states. If that happens, stop, and speak to a qualified teacher or a health professional.
